Use embedded programming techniques to write "bare metal" microcontroller programs in C.
Write interrupt-driven and timer-driven programs.

Design and test basic analog electronic circuits.

slides.title: Beyond the Arduino: 8- and 16-bit microcontrollers
items: Trends are toward faster 32-bit microcontrollers with more memory, etc., though for small projects, (smaller, cheaper, lower-power) 8-bit and 16-bit processors are often adequate, including:
Microchip AVR and PIC
Texas Instruments MSP430
slides.presenterNote: Her 17x slide 23, split in three to fit. Her notes: Arduino is not the only game in town. In the hobby world it's the only game in town (in terms of getting people interested, having lots of fun, Adafruit and others sell a lot of stuff, etc). You are not going to do major embedded systems work on an Arduino Uno. If you want to do industrial stuff you need to up the game. It's not that much more expensive. Trends are: having a microcontroller with 32-bit registers -> more complicated instruction sets, more complex calculations (Arduino: adding to 16-bit numbers takes several clock cycles since you have to break up each number into two 8-bit numbers etc). For a 32-bit microcontroller the arithmetic unit is 32-bits wide, so can multiply two 32-bit numbers in hardware in one clock cycle. That doesn't mean that smaller processors aren't useful (for example, the keypad on your dishwasher is probably handled by an 8-bit processor). Competitor to the AVR is the PIC; now both are under the same company. TI also has one.

slides.title: Beyond the Arduino: ARM architectures
items: ARM designs 32-bit processor architectures (M: microcontrollers, A: microprocessors). Other companies license and manufacture, including:
Microchip SAMD21 (ARM Cortex M0+) and SAMD51 (ARM Cortex M4)
STMicroelectronics (STM32)
Raspberry Pi (RP2040, Pico board)
Silicon Labs (EFM32 Gecko)
NXP
Espressif ESP32 uses a non-ARM architecture
slides.presenterNote: Her 17x slide 23, continued. Her notes: Big dog these days in 32-bit processor design is ARM. They don't actually make chips: they design them and then license the design to companies that fabricate them. They are fabricated in Korea, Taiwan, etc. Xilinx is fabless! They design and then the chips are fabricated elsewhere. Cutting-edge fab stuff is happening just at a handful of companies. But having a bunch of CAD stations and smart people is much cheaper. ARM designs 32-bit and 64-bit architectures. The M0 and M4 are the most commonly seen architectures. You can go out and buy microcontroller chips that are based on these architectures from multiple vendors. They are all based on the same architecture but differ in some other details. You have to look at those differences. Microchip makes the SAMD21 (ARM M0 chip), or SAMD51 (M4) — her slide and note write SAMD52; the M4 part is the SAMD51 (flagged to her). Adafruit makes tiny tiny breakout board with USB connector, STEMMA connector, 48 MHz clock, with ARM chip. There are a whole bunch of Arduino-compatible boards with ARM chips (look like Arduino board, but have M0 or M4 etc chip on them). You can compile and upload Arduino code to them. So great for quick prototyping. So you can try several platforms with the same code-base. STMicroelectronics makes the STM32 (32-bit ARM-based microcontroller). ESP32 (that is your wifi chip) is not an ARM architecture. Espressif (which makes it) is also a fabulous company (in China).

slides.title: Beyond the Arduino: small computers
items: ENGS 62 uses an ARM Cortex-A9 processor.
Raspberry Pi uses 64-bit ARM Cortex-A53 (3B+) and A72 (4) processors. Not microcontrollers, but small computers (run Linux, etc).
Other small single-board computers include support for machine learning. "Edge computing".
slides.presenterNote: Her 17x slide 23, continued. Her notes: ENGS 62 uses an ARM Cortex-A9. A-series is distinguished from M-series (M has lots of pins, timers and stuff) whereas A-series is focussed on computation. Raspberry Pi boards use higher power ARM Cortex (64 bit), they are small computers that can run linux. You can do microcontroller-ish things with them, but what you are really doing is there is a C-program running underneath addressing the pins. NVIDIA makes single-board computer optimized for AI computing. This is a further extension of microcontroller computing called edge computing.

slides.title: Microcontroller "ecosystems"
slides.body: Lots of sources for processor chips and development boards. But a good design depends on more than just a good set of chip specifications, or a low price. You will also need many of these:
items: Development / evaluation boards
Language support (C, C++, Micropython)
Debuggers, emulators (more sophisticated than Arduino)
Real time operating system (RTOS)
Device drivers, APIs, examples
Data sheets and application notes
Developer community, field application engineers
slides.presenterNote: Her 17x slide 25 (her "more that just" typo corrected to "more than"). Her notes: If you want to do a microcontroller project (89-90, etc), there is a lot of sources that want to sell you their very specific board. When you commit to buying a chip you are buying into the entire ecosystem. A good design depends on more than just the chip (and timers etc). You need the ecosystem, for example the prototyping support. A lot of boards sell evaluation boards on which you can prototype without having to solder your circuits etc. An evaluation board is (generally) a basic system built around some specific part, along with all the other stuff you need to get that part to work. Once you stick all these pieces together, and write the software, and it works, you can produce your own circuit board with all the chips on it. Don't look directly for evaluation boards — look for a part you want to have, then look for evaluation boards which have that part or a similar one. Need language support: is there a good compiler? Do they have debuggers? We haven't used this in this class but will be important as you move on. Step-through your code. There is none for the Arduino. Or emulators, that is a piece of software that pretends to be your chip. Do you want a real operating system? In our class we are writing bare-metal C. We are running one thing at a time. This teaches you a lot. Big trend: RTOS which is the compromise between the convenience of a real OS like Linux and the precision of being able to operate in real time. An OS schedules all the different tasks that have to happen. You don't have any control over what happens when. So you are at the mercy of the OS. A RTOS is designed to keep multiple balls in the air but with precise timing that you have control over. You cannot run an RTOS on an Arduino but you can run it on a bigger microcontroller. Device drivers: Adafruit has them for all of their boards. You want that for development! Also want good data sheets and application notes. You want a good developer community and field application engineers that help you use the company's parts and help you solve your problems. You want to know the company is there for you if you need help.
